1.pericope_label: Give unto the Lord, O ye mighty, give unto the Lord glory and strength. Give unto the Lord the glory due unto his name; worship the Lord in the beauty of holiness

schools.summary: Delitzsch grants the thunderstorm as the occasion but will not stop at outward phenomena, since in the psalm the God of redemptive history attests himself; he counts the voice of the Lord seven times, calls it the psalm of the seven thunders, and reports its liturgical place in the second Temple. Ellicott takes benê-elîm literally as sons of gods rather than sons of God, and if the phrase means beings of supernatural power inferior to God then angels is intelligible in the widest sense of ministers, lightning and storm included — so that the forces of nature are being called to praise their own Master.

Calvin explains how the versions went wrong: the Greek translators rendered the phrase twice, once as a vocative and once as an accusative, apparently doubtful which was right, and the Latin and the rest followed them; the correct rendering is 'ye sons of the mighty', a Hebrew idiom for princes. He adds why the great are singled out — David meant to lead all men to worship, but great men are hardest to reduce to order. Gill glosses the glory due to the name as what suits God's nature.

Clarke catalogues the readings of both cruxes — sons of the strong ones or sons of rams, the Chaldee's angels, the Greek and Latin's young rams, the old Psalter's 'sonnes of wether' — collects the versional titles for the psalm, and guesses it commemorates the abundant rain of David's day after three years of drought. On the second he prefers 'the beautiful garments of holiness', and states what the divine name carries: his name is Mercy, his nature love. Wesley keeps the house rather than the dress.

Henry hears the summons aimed at those who hold power by succession, notes that it is repeated three times because the mighty are backward to this duty, and specifies what they must give — themselves first, then crowns laid at his feet, sceptres, swords, keys. Spurgeon insists that neither men nor angels can confer anything on Jehovah, that what men call natural causes are God in action, and that grandees who think it beneath them to fear the Lord have found, when brought to extol him, that their piety was the greatest jewel in their crowns.

Augustine reads the address inward and christologically: bring yourselves, whom the apostles have begotten by the gospel, and worship in a heart enlarged and sanctified, since you are God's royal and holy habitation.

debates.question: Who or what are the benê-elîm summoned in verse 1?

positions.summary: Princes and great men: 'sons of the mighty' is a Hebrew idiom, and the versions' 'sons of rams' arose from the Greek translators rendering the phrase twice and setting down both attempts.

Angels in the widest sense of ministers of God — including the lightning and the storm — since the plural is never used by itself for God as Elohim is; the poet calls the forces of nature to praise their Master.
The readings cannot be settled from the versions, which give sons of the strong ones, sons of rams, hosts of angels, and sons of God indifferently.
The hearers themselves, whom the apostles have begotten by the gospel.
The beautiful garments of holiness — priests and Levites in their best apparel, so that nothing in the service dishonours the divine majesty.
Holy attire, the image taken from the same vestments, so that the presences attending the courts of heaven are bidden to robe themselves as for a high and sacred ceremony.
The holy and beautiful house rather than the dress.
The heart enlarged and sanctified, which is God's royal habitation.

outliers.summary: Quotes the old Psalter's rendering of the disputed phrase — bringes til Lord ye goddes sonnes, brynges til Lord sonnes of wether — with its gloss taking the rams for the hearers themselves, sons of apostles that were leaders of God's folk.
Argues that what men call natural causes are God in action, so that power must never be ascribed to them, and asks that 'all worship be to God only' be emblazoned on every coat of arms.

themes: Give unto the Lord, O ye mighty, give unto the Lord glory and strength.
Give unto the Lord the glory due unto his name; worship the Lord in the beauty of holiness.

3.pericope_label: The voice of the Lord is upon the waters: the God of glory thundereth... The Lord will give strength unto his people; the Lord will bless his people with peace

schools.summary: Ellicott reads the whole of the rest as a single storm tracked geographically — first heard over the waters from the west, breaking on Lebanon and its cedars, moving south to spend its last fury in the whirlwind of sand on the desert, and ending among the acacias and palms near Petra — and closes by treating the last verse as a liturgical addition. Delitzsch refuses to reduce the refrain to an ejaculation meaning 'Hark', since the psalm's theme is the voice of God announcing himself from heaven, and records Luther's attempt to make sense of the Latin at verse 10.

Gill takes every clause twice, the second time allegorically: the voice on the waters is Christ's voice in the gospel reaching many peoples, the flames of fire the cloven tongues at Pentecost, the shaken wilderness the Gentile world convicted by preaching, the calving hinds the churches and ministers by whom souls are brought forth. He keeps the plain sense alongside.

Clarke reads the events as physics: thunder is the voice of the Lord elsewhere in scripture, the many waters are the clouds, and no agent in nature is so powerful as the electric fluid. On the hinds he refuses to go past what the text says and will not meddle with the fables of ancients or moderns. At verse 10 he has Jehovah seated on the deluge appeasing the jarring elements, and prints Virgil's Neptune beside it. Wesley keeps to short glosses.

Spurgeon takes the closing verse for the whole point of the psalm: the power displayed in the hurricane is now promised as the strength of the chosen, and he who wings the unerring bolt will give his redeemed the wings of eagles — asking whether this is not a noble psalm to sing in stormy weather, and whether the reader can sing amid the thunder.

debates.question: What does the repeated word rendered 'voice' carry?

positions.summary: Not an ejaculation meaning 'Hark', which cannot be allowed here since the psalm's theme is the voice of God announcing himself from heaven; the dull sound denotes the thunder, the roar of the tempest, and the thunder of the earthquake besides.
Neither 'Hark' nor thunder alone, but the combined noise of thunder, wind and rain — the gods, in Shakespeare's phrase, that keep this pudder over our heads.
Thunder, called the voice of the Lord elsewhere in scripture and here throughout.

debates.question: Is the storm to be read as a storm?

positions.summary: Yes, and traceable on a map: a single tempest moving from the western waters over Lebanon and south to the desert and the country round Petra.
Yes, and as physics: the electric fluid, the clouds above the firmament, the terror that makes pregnant animals cast their young — with no fables added.
Yes in the letter, but each clause carries a second sense: the gospel reaching the nations, the tongues of Pentecost, the Gentile world shaken by conviction.

outliers.summary: Prints Virgil's description of Neptune calming the sea Juno raised against the fleet of Aeneas alongside verse 10, and asks whether the Roman borrowed some of his chief ideas from this psalm.

Illustrates the shaking of the wilderness from Stanley's account of a desert sandstorm — sheets of sand fleeting along the surface like streams of water, the air filled invisibly and driving in the face like sleet.

themes: The voice of the Lord is upon the waters: the God of glory thundereth: the Lord is upon many waters.
The voice of the Lord is powerful; the voice of the Lord is full of majesty.
The voice of the Lord breaketh the cedars; yea, the Lord breaketh the cedars of Lebanon.
He maketh them also to skip like a calf; Lebanon and Sirion like a young unicorn.
The voice of the Lord divideth the flames of fire.
The voice of the Lord shaketh the wilderness; the Lord shaketh the wilderness of Kadesh.
The voice of the Lord maketh the hinds to calve, and discovereth the forests: and in his temple doth every one speak of his glory.
The Lord sitteth upon the flood; yea, the Lord sitteth King for ever.
The Lord will give strength unto his people; the Lord will bless his people with peace.
